x-m-el-job-01.title: Find the Wrong Line in the Tank Capacity Solution and Check by Estimating
x-m-el-job-01.goal: Learn that converting length units and converting volume units follow different relationships, and check whether a calculated result is reasonable by estimating.
x-m-el-job-01.material: An interior company employee calculated the amount of water needed to fill a rectangular-prism tank that is 2 m long, 50 cm wide and 40 cm high. Below is the employee's solution.
x-m-el-job-01.thinking.0: Find the line that has the error in the solution
x-m-el-job-01.thinking.1: Check by estimating whether the result makes sense
x-m-el-job-01.prereq.0: Length unit relationships such as 1 m = 100 cm
x-m-el-job-01.prereq.1: Finding the volume of a rectangular prism (first-year middle school level)
x-m-el-job-01.prereq.2: The relationship between L and mL
x-m-el-job-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line where the employee's solution first goes wrong.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, mark whether it just carries over the result of the previous line, and what new fact it brings in.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s1.hint.1: Build each new fact (conversion relationship) yourself from 1 m = 100 cm.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s1.line.0: Make the unit m throughout: length 2 m, width 0.5 m, height 0.4 m.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s1.line.2: 1 cubic meter is 100 L, so 0.4 × 100 = 40 L.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s1.line.3: So the tank holds 40 L of water.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s1.explain: The third line is wrong. Just because 1 m is 100 cm does not mean 1 cubic meter is 100 L. In a volume, where lengths are multiplied three times, the conversion ratio is also multiplied three times.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s2.prompt: What is the most reliable check for noticing that the result of 40 L is strange?
x-m-el-job-01.s.s2.hint.0: Repeating the calculation steps is different from estimating the size by a method different from the calculation.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how high the water would be if it spread out over the bottom.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s2.o.a: Calculate the same formula once more in a different order and check that the same value comes out
x-m-el-job-01.s.s2.r.a: If you use the same conversion relationship again, you just get the same value, so a wrong assumption is not revealed.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s2.o.b: Use the area of the tank's bottom to estimate the water height when 40 L is poured in, and compare it with the tank's height
x-m-el-job-01.s.s2.o.c: Check whether the answer comes out as a clean whole number with no decimals, and if so, judge it to be right
x-m-el-job-01.s.s2.r.c: A clean number is different from a correct number. A clean number can come from a wrong assumption too.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s2.explain: The bottom is 2 m × 0.5 m, so it is 1 square meter (= 10,000 square centimeters). If you pour in 40 L = 40,000 cubic centimeters, the water height is only about 4 cm, but the tank is 40 cm high. If you gauge the size by another route outside the solution, the conversion error is revealed.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s3.prompt: What is the correct amount of water? Write where and how to correct it, using the relationship between units as your evidence.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s3.hint.0: Think about how many times larger the volume (three directions) gets when the length becomes 100 times larger.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s3.hint.1: If you know one relationship between cubic centimeters and L, connect it first.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain how the corrected conversion (1 cubic meter = 1000 L) comes from the length conversion (1 m = 100 cm)?
x-m-el-job-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Besides the conversion rule, did you also use an estimate of size as evidence that 40 L is wrong?
x-m-el-job-01.s.s3.model.0: 1 cubic meter is 1000 L. So 0.4 cubic meters is 400 L, and if it were 40 L, the water would be only 4 cm high on the bottom (2 m × 0.5 m), which makes no sense.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s3.model.1: Since 1 m is 100 cm, 1 cubic meter is 100×100×100 = 1,000,000 cubic centimeters, and 1 L is 1000 cubic centimeters, so 1 cubic meter = 1000 L. So 0.4 × 1000 = 400 L.
x-m-el-job-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: You derived the conversion relationship directly from the length units.

x-m-el-job-02.title: Saying the Same Speed in Two Units
x-m-el-job-02.goal: Using the conversion between speed per minute (m) and speed per hour (km), find on your own the condition under which both values are natural numbers, and explain why.
x-m-el-job-02.material: Two people in a running club described the same speed in different units. One said 'x m per minute' (the distance covered in 1 minute), and the other said 'y km per hour' (the distance covered in 1 hour). They want to state the numbers only as natural numbers, with no decimals or fractions.
x-m-el-job-02.thinking.1: Make several examples that satisfy a condition
x-m-el-job-02.thinking.2: Generalize the condition for being a natural number
x-m-el-job-02.prereq.1: Speed is expressed as the distance covered in the same amount of time (middle school level)
x-m-el-job-02.s.s1.prompt: About how many meters per minute is the speed of a person running at 6 km per hour? First estimate the size.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s1.hint.0: First change the distance covered in 1 hour into m.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s1.hint.1: Divide that distance by 60 minutes to estimate the distance covered in 1 minute.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s1.r.a: Check whether it takes about 10 minutes to go 1 km. Check the direction in which you change the units.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s1.r.c: 1000 m per minute corresponds to 60 km per hour. Check the ratio of 1 minute to 1 hour.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s1.explain: 6 km per hour is 6000 m in 1 hour, and 1 hour is 60 minutes, so it is about 100 m in 1 minute.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different pairs of natural numbers, speed per minute x (m) and speed per hour y (km), that make the same speed. The speed per hour is from 6 to 20 inclusive (the range a person can run).
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.hint.0: Express in km the distance covered in 1 hour at x m per minute.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.hint.1: Fix one speed per hour and check whether the speed per minute is a natural number.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.hint.2: If some speeds per hour do not give natural numbers, look for what those speeds have in common.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.fail.c1: x and y must be natural numbers.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The two values are the same speed.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.fail.c2: x m per minute and y km per hour are not the same speed. Compare the distance covered in 1 hour in the same unit.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The speed per hour is within the range.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The speed per hour must be from 6 to 20 inclusive.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.explain: 100 m per minute is 6000 m in 1 hour, so it is 6 km per hour. Each time the speed per minute increases by 50 m, the speed per hour increases by 3 km. So 100/6, 150/9, 200/12, 250/15, 300/18 are the possible pairs.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain why 7 km or 8 km per hour does not work, but 6, 9 and 12 km do.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: When you change y km per hour to speed per minute, it becomes a fraction. See what y has to be like for the denominator to divide evenly.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Calculate the speed per minute for 7 and 8 directly, and find why they become decimals.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If you change the speed per hour into speed per minute, ...
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the pairs you made follow the same rule?
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the reason for the rule by asking 'why 3 (or 50) in particular?'
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.because.model.0: y km per hour in speed per minute is 1000×y÷60 = 50y/3 m. For this to be a natural number, y has to be a multiple of 3, so 6, 9, 12 work and 7, 8 do not.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.because.model.1: x m per minute is 60x m = 0.06x km in 1 hour. For both to be integers, x has to be a multiple of 50, and then the speed per hour goes up by 3 each time.
x-m-el-job-02.s.s2.because.model.2: Converting speed y per hour to per minute gives 50y/3, so y must be divisible by 3 to be a natural number. 6, 9, and 12 work, and 7 and 8 do not.

x-m-el-job-03.title: Judging the Actual Area of a Room from a Scale Drawing
x-m-el-job-03.goal: Learn that the scale for length and the scale for area are different, and pick out the valid one by evaluating different estimates.
x-m-el-job-03.material:
In a floor plan with a scale of 1:200, a room is a rectangle 5 cm long and 4 cm wide. Four students each calculated the room's actual area.
A: Multiply the drawing's area of 20 square centimeters by 200 to get 4000 square centimeters, which is 0.4 square meters.
B: The actual length is 10 m and the width is 8 m, so it is 80 square meters.
C: Multiply the drawing's area of 20 square centimeters by 200×200 to get 800,000 square centimeters, which is 80 square meters.
D: The actual length is 1000 cm and the width is 800 cm, so it is 800,000 square centimeters, and since 1 square meter is 100 square centimeters, it is 8000 square meters.
x-m-el-job-03.thinking.0: Compare and evaluate the validity of several claims
x-m-el-job-03.thinking.1: Tell the ratio of lengths from the ratio of areas
x-m-el-job-03.thinking.2: Write an explanation that refutes a misconception
x-m-el-job-03.prereq.0: The meaning of a scale of 1:200 (the ratio showing how many actual cm 1 cm on the drawing is)
x-m-el-job-03.prereq.1: 1 m = 100 cm, the area of a rectangle
x-m-el-job-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the students whose calculations found the actual area validly. (A to D in the options are the students' names in the information above.)
x-m-el-job-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each calculation, find the actual length and width yourself and compare the area you get with their value.
x-m-el-job-03.s.s1.hint.1: For calculations that gave different results, mark which step is different.
x-m-el-job-03.s.s1.o.a: A: Multiply the drawing's area by 200 to get 4000 square centimeters, which is 0.4 square meters
x-m-el-job-03.s.s1.r.a: This thinks that area, like length, only needs to be multiplied by 200. It missed that the length and the width each get bigger.
x-m-el-job-03.s.s1.o.b: B: The actual length is 10 m and the width is 8 m, so it is 80 square meters
x-m-el-job-03.s.s1.explain: The actual length is 10 m and the width is 8 m, so the area is 80 square meters (B). Multiplying the drawing's area by 200×200 = 40,000 gives the same value (C). A multiplied the area by only 200, and D used a wrong conversion of 100 between square meters and square centimeters (1 square meter = 10,000 square centimeters).
x-m-el-job-03.s.s2.prompt: Explain to Student A 'why the area is not 200 times.' Write it by comparing the room in the drawing with the actual room.
x-m-el-job-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write down what the actual length is when the length on the drawing is 5 cm, and what the actual width is.
x-m-el-job-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the area of a rectangle where only the length is made 200 times larger with the area of one where both length and width are made 200 times larger.
x-m-el-job-03.s.s2.placeholder: Example: If the length is 200 times, the length and the width ...
x-m-el-job-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you explain in words how the length and the width each become 200 times larger?
x-m-el-job-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check your explanation by connecting it to the value of 80 square meters?
x-m-el-job-03.s.s2.model.0: For area, both the length and the width become 200 times larger, so it is not 200 times but 200×200 = 40000 times. So 20 square centimeters times 40000 is 800,000 square centimeters, which is 80 square meters.
x-m-el-job-03.s.s2.model.1: If the ratio of lengths is 1:200, the ratio of areas is its square. Both the length and the width get 200 times larger, so the area becomes 40,000 times larger.
x-m-el-job-03.s.s1.o.c: 다: multiply the area on the drawing by 200×200 to get 800,000 square centimeters, that is, 80 square meters
x-m-el-job-03.s.s1.o.d: 라: it is 800,000 square centimeters, and 1 square meter is 100 square centimeters, so 8000 square meters
x-m-el-job-03.s.s1.r.d: You applied the relationship between length units (100 times) directly to area units. Consider the case where both the width and the length become 100 times as long.
x-m-el-job-03.s.s2.model.2: If the length is multiplied by 200, the area is multiplied by 200 squared. Student 가 found the area by multiplying in only one direction by 200.

x-m-el-job-04.title: A Copied Floor Plan: Can We Trust the Scale as It Is?
x-m-el-job-04.goal: Learn that the scale printed on a drawing can change through copying or shrinking, and learn how to revise your judgment as new information comes in.
x-m-el-job-04.material: You want to find the length of a living room from a floor plan of an apartment printed in a sales brochure. On the plan, the living room is 6 cm long.
x-m-el-job-04.thinking.0: Revise your judgment with new information
x-m-el-job-04.thinking.1: Tell apart the scale notation and the actual size of the drawing
x-m-el-job-04.thinking.2: Check the ratio with a length bar
x-m-el-job-04.prereq.0: The meaning of scale (the ratio between length on the drawing and actual length)
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, make your judgment with the information up to that point.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write in one line 'what has changed.'
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.hint.1: Think about which one changes together when copying: the scale notation or the length bar.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.0.info: At the top of the floor plan it says 'Scale 1:100.' The living room's length on the plan is 6 cm.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: With the information now, how would you judge the living room's length?
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.0.after: With a scale of 1:100, 6 cm is 600 cm = 6 m. For now, this is a reasonable judgment.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Decide it is 6 m and start arranging the furniture
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Checking the notation is good, but you have not yet checked whether the notation matches the drawing's current size.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Consider it to be about 6 m, but want to check whether the plan is at its original size
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: No length is written, so it cannot be known
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: With the length on the drawing and the scale, you can make an estimate.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.1.info: There is small print in the corner of the brochure: 'This floor plan is an A3 original copied onto A4 at 70% size.'
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: With this information, how will the living room's actual length compare with 6 m?
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.1.after: The plan was shrunk to 70%, so in the original it was 6 ÷ 0.7 ≈ 8.57 cm. So the actual length is about 8.6 m, which is longer than 6 m.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It will be shorter than 6 m
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You may have thought the wrong way around about the direction in which the drawing shrank and the direction in which the actual size grows.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It will be longer than 6 m
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is still 6 m, because the written scale stays the same even when copied
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The printed number stays the same when copied, but the length on the drawing shrinks. Tell apart which has changed, the number or the length.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Below the floor plan there is a length bar (a line segment showing an actual 5 m). You measure it with a ruler and the segment is 3.5 cm long.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: About how long is the living room's actual length?
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.2.after: 3.5 cm is 5 m, so 1 cm is about 1.43 m, and 6 cm is about 8.57 m. This is the same as the calculation in the second step. The length bar shrinks along with the drawing when it is shrunk, so it is a safe reference.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This may be the value from multiplying the ratio the wrong way around. First find how many m 1 cm is.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is the value from using the scale notation as it is. Compare it with the length bar.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s1.reflect: At first you judged by the scale notation alone. When the copying information came in, you learned that the notation and the actual size of the drawing can differ, and you checked this with the length bar. When new information appears, look at which assumption of your earlier judgment breaks.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s2.prompt: Write one thing you must check before buying furniture, trusting the brochure or the lengths on the drawing, and the reason.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s2.hint.0: Separate what stays the same when the drawing is copied from what shrinks together with it.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what assumptions you can do without when you use a length bar to find the ratio.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you distinguish between whether what you checked is the scale number or the actual length on the drawing?
x-m-el-job-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is the reason you gave connected to the information in this problem (70% copy)?
x-m-el-job-04.s.s2.model.0: Don't trust only the scale number; measure with the length bar on the drawing yourself. If the size changes when copying, the number stays the same but becomes wrong.
x-m-el-job-04.s.s2.model.1: You must check whether the plan was printed at its original size. If it is printed shrunk or enlarged, the number 1:100 no longer fits and you may get the actual length wrong.

x-m-el-job-05.title: Fitting the Presentation Order to the Conditions
x-m-el-job-05.topic: Counting cases and planning a schedule
x-m-el-job-05.goal: Make presentation orders that satisfy all the conditions, and explain how you counted the total number of possible orders without missing any.
x-m-el-job-05.material:
At a festival stage, clubs A, B, C and D each perform once, one after another. The conditions are as follows.
① A cannot be first because of equipment setup.
② D cannot be last because of another commitment.
③ B's video serves as the background for C's performance, so B must perform before C.
Order number 1 is first and 4 is last.
x-m-el-job-05.thinking.1: Count without missing any by splitting into conditions
x-m-el-job-05.thinking.2: Explain how you became sure of the count
x-m-el-job-05.prereq.0: The experience that arranging 4 things in a row produces different arrangements
x-m-el-job-05.prereq.1: The basics of counting by splitting up (the sum rule level)
x-m-el-job-05.s.s1.prompt: If only condition ③ (B before C) is kept, how many presentation orders are there for the 4 clubs in all?
x-m-el-job-05.s.s1.hint.0: First recall how many orders there are with no conditions at all.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s1.hint.1: See what happens when you swap B's and C's places in an order.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s1.r.a: It does not reflect that condition ③ restricts the order.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s1.r.b: Look back at how you counted that B and C's before-and-after relationship is settled as one of two.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s1.explain: There are 24 orders for the 4 clubs in all, and swapping B and C's before-and-after pairs them up. Exactly half of them, 12 ways, satisfy condition ③.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different presentation orders that satisfy all three conditions. a, b, c and d are the order numbers (1 to 4) of A, B, C and D respectively. The four clubs' numbers must all be different.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.hint.0: Start by placing the club with the most restrictions.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.hint.1: Work out what happens to the remaining places if you put B at 1.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.hint.2: After making an order, check it against conditions ①, ② and ③ one by one.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.ok.c1: All are natural numbers from 1 to 4.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The order numbers must be natural numbers from 1 to 4.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Two clubs cannot use the same order.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.fail.c3: A cannot be in the first position (condition ①).
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.fail.c4: D cannot be in the last position (condition ②).
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.fail.c5: B must perform before C (condition ③).
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.explain: There are 7 orders in all that satisfy the conditions. Written as orders, they are BADC, BCDA, BDAC, BDCA, DABC, DBAC, DBCA. For example, BADC means A=2, B=1, C=4, D=3.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Find out how many possible orders there are in all, and write the method that made you sure you missed none.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: See how many cases there are if you split by which club can be in the first position.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: In each case, write one by one how to place the other three clubs to fit the conditions.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that your counting method does not count the same order twice?
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Are the 3 orders you made among the 7 you counted?
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.because.model.0: If you split into the case where B is first with 4 ways and the case where D is first with 3 ways, there are 7 in all.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.because.model.1: From the 12 ways in which B is before C, remove the 3 where A is first, then remove the 2 more where D is last, and 7 remain.
x-m-el-job-05.s.s2.because.model.2: Split by which team can come first. If B is first there are 4 ways, and if D is first there are 3 ways, so there are 7 ways in all.

x-m-el-job-06.title: Fixing a Solution on Counting Activity Schedules
x-m-el-job-06.topic: Counting cases and planning a schedule
x-m-el-job-06.goal: Tell apart cases with order from cases without order, find and fix the error in a solution counting schedule assignments, and check using another method.
x-m-el-job-06.material: On a field trip day, you choose 3 of 5 activities (A, B, C, D, E) and assign one to each of the morning, afternoon and evening time slots. Activity A is outdoors, so it cannot be done in the evening. A student solved how many possible assignments there are in all.
x-m-el-job-06.thinking.0: Find the error in the solution
x-m-el-job-06.thinking.1: Tell apart whether order matters and fix it
x-m-el-job-06.prereq.0: The product rule (counting by multiplying choices made in several steps)
x-m-el-job-06.prereq.1: The basics of the number of ways to choose some from n different things
x-m-el-job-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line where the student's solution first goes wrong.
x-m-el-job-06.s.s1.line.0: We choose 3 of 5 and assign them to morning, afternoon and evening, so 5×4×3 = 60 ways.
x-m-el-job-06.s.s1.line.2: So the number of cases where A is not assigned to the evening is 60 − 6 = 54 ways.
x-m-el-job-06.s.s2.prompt: Find the correct number of ways, and show that another method (such as deciding the evening slot first) gives the same value.
x-m-el-job-06.s.s2.hint.0: Count by multiplication the ways to fill the morning and afternoon places one at a time in the case where A is in the evening.
x-m-el-job-06.s.s2.hint.1: Try deciding the evening slot first and then filling in the rest.
x-m-el-job-06.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Morning and afternoon have an order, so ...
x-m-el-job-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the value from the other method equals 48?
x-m-el-job-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the reason for telling morning and afternoon apart using the schedule situation?
x-m-el-job-06.s.s2.model.1: For the evening, we choose one of the 4 other than A, which is 4 ways, and the ways to set the morning and afternoon from the remaining 4 is 4×3, so 4×4×3 = 48 ways.
x-m-el-job-06.s.s1.hint.0: First consider whether a schedule with activity X in the morning and activity Y in the afternoon is the same schedule as one with Y in the morning and X in the afternoon.
x-m-el-job-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare line by line in order whether that criterion is applied the same way in every line of the solution.
x-m-el-job-06.s.s1.line.1: Count the cases where A is assigned to the evening. The number of ways to choose the 2 activities for the morning and afternoon from the other 4 is (4×3)÷2 = 6.
x-m-el-job-06.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is off. Morning and afternoon are different time slots, so even the same two activities make different schedules depending on which is in the morning. But this line divides (4×3) by 2, counting without distinguishing the order, so the value is cut in half.
x-m-el-job-06.s.s2.model.0: Morning and afternoon have an order, so you should not divide by 2, and it is 4×3 = 12. So 60 − 12 = 48.

x-m-el-job-07.title: Comparing Paint Quantity Estimates
x-m-el-job-07.topic: Validity of cost and material calculations
x-m-el-job-07.goal: See why different estimation methods reach the same conclusion, and find on your own the conditions under which an estimate is safe and the conditions under which the conclusion changes.
x-m-el-job-07.material:
You want to paint only the four walls of a room that is 4 m long, 3 m wide and 2.5 m high, twice (2 coats). The windows and door together have an area of 3.2 square meters and are not painted. 1 L of paint covers 10 square meters in one coat, and it is sold only in 4 L cans. Four people estimated the number of cans needed in different ways.
A: The floor is 4×3 = 12 square meters, so painting 12 square meters twice is 24 square meters, 2.4 L, so 1 can.
B: The wall area of 35 square meters minus 3.2 is 31.8, two coats is 63.6 square meters, 6.36 L, so 2 cans.
C: Ignoring the windows and door, painting 35 square meters twice is 70 square meters, 7 L, so 2 cans.
D: Painting 31.8 square meters only once is 3.18 L, so 1 can.
x-m-el-job-07.thinking.0: Evaluate the validity of several estimating methods
x-m-el-job-07.thinking.1: How the difference between an approximation and an exact value affects the conclusion
x-m-el-job-07.thinking.2: Make cases where the conclusion differs
x-m-el-job-07.prereq.0: Finding the wall area (side area) of a rectangular-prism room
x-m-el-job-07.prereq.1: Decimal multiplication and division, rounding up to decide a count
x-m-el-job-07.s.s1.hint.1: After finding the L needed, compare down to how many cans (4 L each) you must buy.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s1.o.a: D: Painting 31.8 square meters once is 3.18 L, so 1 can
x-m-el-job-07.s.s1.r.a: If you leave out the condition of the problem (2 coats), the amount needed is cut in half. Check the conditions one by one.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s1.o.b: B: Painting the walls of 31.8 square meters twice is 6.36 L, so 2 cans
x-m-el-job-07.s.s1.o.c: A: Painting the floor of 12 square meters twice is 2.4 L, so 1 can
x-m-el-job-07.s.s1.r.c: What is painted is the walls. Check which surface's area is being used.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s1.o.d: C: Not subtracting the windows and door and painting 35 square meters twice gives 7 L, 2 cans
x-m-el-job-07.s.s1.explain: What is painted is the four walls, with 2 coats. B reasoned exactly, and 6.36 L needs 2 cans of 4 L (8 L). C ignored the windows and door and got 7 L, but the number of cans is the same, 2. A used the floor, and D left out the 2-coat condition.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write the area of wall to be painted using w, and express the L needed for two coats as a formula in w.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.var.w: Total area of windows and door w (square meters)
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.fail.c2: At this w, 1 can is not enough. Multiply the area to be painted by two coats and work out the L needed.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.explain: The wall area to be painted is 35−w square meters with 2 coats, so the L needed is (35−w)×2÷10. For this to be 4 L or less, w has to be 15 or more. If the windows and door are 15 or more out of a room's 35 square meters of wall, nearly half of the wall is window.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain why an estimate that does not subtract the windows and door, as in C, is a 'safe estimate,' and what its limits are.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Think about whether ignoring the windows makes the area to be painted larger or smaller than it really is.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Imagine what happens if the size of the room or of the windows changes.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: If you do not subtract the windows, ...
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you tell apart whether the estimate errs on the 'generous side' or on the 'short side'?
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you state the condition under which the limit arises with a number (the value of w)?
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.because.model.0: If you do not subtract the windows, you estimate a larger area than the real one, so you will never come up short and it is safe, but if the windows are very big, one can may be left over, which is a waste.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.because.model.1: If you do not subtract the windows and door area, the amount needed comes out larger, so there is some margin. But if the windows are 15 square meters or more, in reality 1 can would do, yet you would buy 2 cans.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the opinions whose conclusion matches the number of cans actually needed (the value found considering all the conditions of the problem).
x-m-el-job-07.s.s1.hint.0: First find for yourself the number of cans needed by applying all the conditions of the problem (what is painted, the number of coats, the parts to exclude), then compare it one by one with the number of cans each opinion gave.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.prompt: If you ignore windows and doors as 다 does, 2 cans are needed, but make a case where 1 can is actually enough. Enter 2 different values of w, the total area of the windows and doors (square meters), each at least 10 and at most 30. Imagine a room where large glass windows take up a big part of the wall. (The wall area is 35 square meters, 2 coats, 10 square meters per 1 L, 4 L cans)
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.hint.1: Pick one w, calculate the number of L needed, and find how many cans are needed. If you get 2 cans, change w and check again.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.fail.c1: w must be at least 10 and at most 30.
x-m-el-job-07.s.s2.because.model.2: It calculates a larger area than the real one, so you never run short. The limitation is that if the windows are very large, the number of cans can go up by one and money can be wasted.

x-m-el-job-08.title: The Rounding Error in a Tile Estimate
x-m-el-job-08.topic: Validity of cost and material calculations
x-m-el-job-08.goal: Understand why rounding up is needed for materials you can buy only by the piece, and find on your own cases where ordinary rounding causes a shortage.
x-m-el-job-08.material: You are laying square tiles with 30 cm sides on the floor of a room that is 3.6 m long and 4.1 m wide. Tiles are sold only in boxes of 10, and one box costs 18,000원. Every tile is used as a whole piece, and loss from cutting is not considered. Below is a student's estimate solution.
x-m-el-job-08.thinking.0: Find the error in the estimate solution
x-m-el-job-08.thinking.1: Check whether the mathematical handling fits real-life constraints
x-m-el-job-08.thinking.2: Find the conditions under which the error occurs
x-m-el-job-08.prereq.0: The relationship between square centimeters and square meters
x-m-el-job-08.prereq.1: The meaning of rounding, rounding up and rounding down
x-m-el-job-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line of the estimate solution that has a problem.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s1.hint.0: Look separately at whether each line's calculation is right and whether the way it was handled fits the condition 'sold only by the box.'
x-m-el-job-08.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate how many tiles you can actually lay with 16 boxes.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s1.line.0: The room's area is 3.6 × 4.1 = 14.76 square meters.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s1.line.1: One tile is 30 cm × 30 cm = 900 square centimeters = 0.09 square meters.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s1.line.3: There are 10 tiles per box, so 164 ÷ 10 = 16.4, and rounding gives 16 boxes to buy.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is the problem. 16 boxes is 160 tiles, so it is 4 tiles short. For materials sold only in boxes, you must round up so you do not fall short. Then it is 17 boxes, and the cost is 17 × 18,000 = 306,000원.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.prompt: Say the number of tiles needed is n. Make 3 different values of n for which rounding the number of boxes causes a shortage of tiles. (n is a natural number from 100 to 300)
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.hint.0: For n=164, 160 and 167, find n÷10 and compare how many tiles the rounded number of boxes gives.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.hint.1: Look for what the values of n that cause a shortage have in common in their ones digit.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number within the range.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number from 100 to 300.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.ok.c2: Rounding causes a shortage of boxes.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.fail.c2: For this n, rounding does not cause a shortage. See what happens to the decimal part of the quotient when rounding.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.explain: If the decimal part of n divided by 10 is 0.1 to 0.4, rounding goes down and there are not enough boxes. Values of n with a ones digit of 1 to 4 are such cases. If the ones digit is 5 to 9, rounding gives the same as rounding up, and if it is 0, it fits exactly.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain why you should round up, not use ordinary rounding, when finding the number of boxes.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare what problem arises when there are too few boxes and when there are extra boxes.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare 16 boxes and 17 boxes using the example of 164 tiles.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: Boxes cannot be bought one tile at a time, so ...
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is the rule about the ones digit of the n you made connected with the reason?
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write why you round up even though that leaves extra tiles?
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.because.model.0: With rounding, when the ones digit is 1 to 4 there are not enough boxes. Even if there are leftover tiles, you have to buy one more box, so you should round up.
x-m-el-job-08.s.s2.because.model.1: Boxes cannot be bought as single tiles, so with 164 tiles, 16 boxes (160 tiles) is 4 tiles short. So you should always round up.

x-m-el-job-09.title: Cookie Sale: What More Do We Need to Know to Calculate?
x-m-el-job-09.goal: Judge whether you can calculate with only the information given in the problem, choose what information is missing, and find a conclusion with the new information.
x-m-el-job-09.material: A club plans to sell handmade cookies at a festival, all at 1,500원 each. They have already spent 36,000원 on ingredients. The club president asked, 'Please calculate how many we have to sell so that we don't lose money.'
x-m-el-job-09.thinking.1: Telling needed information from unneeded information
x-m-el-job-09.thinking.2: Judging the break-even condition by understanding the numbers
x-m-el-job-09.prereq.0: The meaning of revenue, expense and profit
x-m-el-job-09.prereq.1: The basics of linear expressions and inequalities
x-m-el-job-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything you still need to know before you can calculate.
x-m-el-job-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write as a formula which items produce profit and which items are subtracted.
x-m-el-job-09.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the formula changes with and without the information in each option.
x-m-el-job-09.s.s1.o.a: Whether there are other fixed expenses besides the ingredient cost, such as a booth fee
x-m-el-job-09.s.s1.o.b: How many kinds of cookies were made
x-m-el-job-09.s.s1.r.b: If all cookies are the same price, the number of kinds does not affect profit or loss. Think about which information changes profit and loss.
x-m-el-job-09.s.s1.o.c: Whether there is a separate packaging cost each time a cookie is sold
x-m-el-job-09.s.s1.o.d: How many cookies were prepared in total
x-m-el-job-09.s.s1.r.d: The number prepared is needed to see 'whether it is possible within that.' Think about whether it is truly needed to find the minimum number to sell so as not to lose money.
x-m-el-job-09.s.s1.explain: To avoid a loss, (selling price per cookie − extra cost per cookie) multiplied by the number sold must be at least the total fixed expenses. So you need to know the fixed expenses (booth fee and so on) and the extra cost per cookie (packaging). The number of kinds does not matter if the price is the same, and the number prepared is used to see whether it is possible.
x-m-el-job-09.s.s1.acc.0: The number of cookies prepared is not needed to find the minimum number to sell, but it is needed to judge whether that goal is realistically possible.
x-m-el-job-09.s.s2.prompt: You found out that the booth fee is 4,000원, the packaging cost is 300원 per cookie, and 60 cookies were prepared. Write the minimum number you have to sell so as not to lose money, and the profit if you sell all 60.
x-m-el-job-09.s.s2.hint.0: First find the selling price minus the cost per cookie.
x-m-el-job-09.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how to handle the quotient of the fixed expenses divided by that value so that there is 'no loss.'
x-m-el-job-09.s.s2.placeholder: Example: The money left per cookie is ...
x-m-el-job-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you find and write the money left per cookie and the fixed expenses separately?
x-m-el-job-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why 33 is not enough (how you handled the quotient 33.3…)?
x-m-el-job-09.s.s2.model.0: 1,500−300 = 1,200원 is left per cookie and the fixed expenses are 36,000+4,000 = 40,000원, so 40,000÷1,200 = 33.3…, so you have to sell at least 34. If you sell all 60, the profit is 72,000−40,000 = 32,000원.
x-m-el-job-09.s.s2.model.1: The money left per cookie is 1,200원 and the total expenses are 40,000원. With 33 it is 39,600원, which is short, and from 34 on there is no loss. If you sell all 60, 32,000원 is left.

x-m-el-job-10.title: Choosing a Phone Plan: Is One Month of Information Enough?
x-m-el-job-10.goal: Learn that one or two months of data are not enough to choose a plan, and that the better plan changes when usage changes, and find the boundary.
x-m-el-job-10.material: You want to use one of two mobile phone plans from now on. Plan A costs 30,000원 a month and includes up to 10 GB of data, with 5,000원 per GB for anything over. Plan B costs 42,000원 a month and has unlimited data. Usage is calculated only in whole GB.
x-m-el-job-10.thinking.0: Revise your judgment as information grows
x-m-el-job-10.thinking.1: Find the boundary condition (where the order reverses)
x-m-el-job-10.thinking.2: Judge whether a sample is sufficient
x-m-el-job-10.prereq.0: Expressing fees with linear expressions (middle school level)
x-m-el-job-10.prereq.1: The meaning of total and average
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, make your judgment with the information up to that point.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.hint.0: Write down both plans' fees for each month and compare the totals.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.hint.1: Estimate about where the usage is at which the fees of A and B become equal.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.0.info: Last month's data usage was 9 GB.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: If you chose a plan to use from now on, how would you judge?
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.0.after: With 9 GB last month, A is 30,000원 and B is 42,000원, so A is cheaper. But this is data for only one month.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: B: unlimited, so I can relax
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Feeling relaxed is different from costing less. Calculate last month's fee on both plans.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: A: based on last month, it is cheaper
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It's only one month of data, so it's still hard to decide
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.1.info: This month you watched a lot of videos and used 12 GB.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: With the information from these two months, how would you revise your judgment?
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.1.after: With 12 GB, A is 30,000 + 2×5,000 = 40,000원, which is still cheaper than B (42,000원). Even when you go over, B does not become better right away.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Keep A: it was cheaper this month too
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Switch to B: you went over 10 GB, so B is better now
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Going over 10 GB does not make B better right away. Calculate the fee for the extra amount.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Two months of data is still too early
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.2.info: The expected usage for the next 4 months is 8 GB, 13 GB, 14 GB and 15 GB.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which plan has the lower total fee over these 4 months?
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.2.after: A is 30,000 + 45,000 + 50,000 + 55,000 = 180,000원 and B is 42,000×4 = 168,000원. A looked cheaper in the first two months, but when months with increased usage are mixed in, B is cheaper.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Just because A is cheaper in some months does not mean its total is cheaper. Calculate A's fee for each month and add them up.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The two plans are the same
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Deciding they are the same before finding the total lacks evidence.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s1.reflect: With one month and two months of data, A looked better, but once you saw the distribution of future usage, your judgment changed. Think about what more information you need before fixing your judgment, and at what usage the better plan changes.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different values of monthly usage x GB for which Plan B is cheaper than Plan A. (x is an integer from 0 to 40)
x-m-el-job-10.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate A's fee in turn for x=10, 11, 12, 13.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s2.hint.1: Find where x is when A's fee first goes over 42,000원.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer within the range.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be an integer from 0 to 40.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s2.ok.c2: A's fee is more expensive than B's.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s2.fail.c2: At this usage, A is cheaper than or equal to B. Add the fee for the extra amount as well.
x-m-el-job-10.s.s2.explain: A's fee is 30,000 + 5,000×(x−10). It goes over 42,000원 when x is 13 or more. At x=12 it is 40,000원 and A is still cheaper, and at 13 it is 45,000원 and B becomes cheaper.
